In the Southern banana salamander, embryos maintained at an experimental temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] complete their development and hatch after approximately 30 days [ab = approximately 30 days], a duration that is consistent with the relatively accelerated embryogenesis observed in many small-bodied neotropical plethodontids. At the moment of hatching, the newly emerged larvae possess a wet weight at birth of roughly 0.0141 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.0141 grams], a value that reflects the modest yolk reserves contained within the ova, which for this species approximately 3 millimeters in diameter. This initial body mass is remarkably low when compared to the ultimate wet weight of 1.35 grams [Wwi = 1.35 grams] that sexually mature individuals ultimately attain, indicating a substantial post-hatching growth phase spanning several orders of magnitude. The transition from a non-feeding, yolk-dependent larva to an exogenously feeding, gill-breathing tadpole marks a critical energetic shift, after which the individual must secure food resources to sustain its rapid somatic development under the controlled thermal conditions of the laboratory.

Basal oxygen consumption in this tropical salamander, measured at rest in post-absorptive adults, was determined to be 0.0003 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 0.0003 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a stable ambient temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This metabolic rate, corresponding to the maximum basal metabolic rate, ranks among the lowest recorded for any terrestrial amphibian of comparable adult body size, a finding that aligns with the generally low metabolic demands of lungless salamanders that rely entirely on cutaneous respiration. The extraordinarily small value underscores the species’ energy-conserving life history strategy, wherein routine metabolic expenditure is minimized, allowing resources to be channeled preferentially into somatic growth and eventual reproductive output. Such a low resting metabolism is likely an adaptation to the humid, thermally stable microhabitats of the tropical cloud forest floor, where energy availability can be seasonally unpredictable but thermal conditions remain remarkably constant.

Reproductive output in this species, extrapolated from data on the congener Bolitoglossa mexicana and corrected for the smaller body size of B. occidentalis, is estimated to be 15 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 15 eggs per clutch] when females are maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. Given that individual females are believed to produce only a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], the maximum reproductive rate thus yields an annual output of 15 eggs, a modest fecundity typical of many direct-developing or semi-direct-developing plethodontids that invest heavily in relatively large, yolk-rich ova rather than numerous small ones. This low reproductive frequency suggests that each breeding event represents a significant energetic investment for the female, who must accumulate sufficient lipid stores to provision the developing oocytes over an extended vitellogenic period. The trade-off between clutch size and offspring quality is evident, as the relatively large egg diameter of 3 millimeters confers a substantial initial size advantage to the hatchling.

Longevity records suggest that the maximum lifespan for this species is 35 years [am = 35 years], a figure borrowed from the closely related Bolitoglossa mexicana and considered applicable to B at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. occidentalis given their similar body sizes and life histories. At the standard temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], this exceptionally long lifespan—remarkable for an amphibian of merely 1.35 grams [Wwi = 1.35 grams]—places the Southern banana salamander among the most long-lived of all known salamanders relative to its body mass. Such extreme longevity is typically associated with a slow life-history pace, characterized by delayed maturation, infrequent reproduction, and low annual mortality rates in the stable, predator-limited environments of neotropical montane forests. The capacity for such prolonged survival likely requires robust cellular maintenance mechanisms and efficient antioxidant defenses, adaptations that are subjects of ongoing comparative gerontological research within the Bolitoglossinae.

Females of Bolitoglossa occidentalis that have completed metamorphosis require approximately 3 years following metamorphosis [tp = approximately 3 years following metamorphosis] to reach sexual maturity, a protracted interval that aligns with the slow life-history strategy of neotropical montane plethodontids, measured at a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This protracted period of post-metamorphic maturation, during which the juvenile transforms into a reproductively active adult, contrasts sharply with the brief larval phase but is consistent with the species’ overall slow life history. During this time, the sub-adult must nearly achieve its asymptotic adult body mass while navigating the challenges of foraging in the leaf litter and avoiding predation. The delay in the onset of gonadal maturation likely reflects the time required to accumulate sufficient energy reserves to support the production of a clutch of 15 large eggs, a strategy that prioritizes future reproductive success over early breeding. This extended juvenile period is a common feature of tropical montane plethodontids, where resource availability is low but environmental stability is high.
